one_line: Write full sentences. Give each point its reason or detail. Answer the question on the paper, about the scenario it gives.

points.text: No Cambridge document for 9626 tells you to answer in bullet points. The Cambridge guide for students says the opposite.

cites.quote: Answer the questions in sentences. Never give ‘one word’ or one ‘phrase’ answers.

points.text: Examiner reports repeat this advice in almost every exam series. Use full sentences for Describe and Explain answers too, as well as for the long questions.

cites.quote: Candidates should also be encouraged to write full sentences and discouraged from writing bulleted, short statements in their responses. Descriptions or explanations can only be conveyed in full sentences.
Candidates should write full sentences and avoid bulleted short statements in their responses.

points.text: The real problem with bullets is what they leave out. A bullet is usually a bare point with no reason or detail. Most of the marks are for the reason or detail.

cites.quote: the use of bullet points rarely produces little more than simple points or short statements with no explanations or descriptions
Short statements or bulleted responses that do not expand on facts cannot be awarded the higher marks because these are not discussions.

points.text: For Discuss, Evaluate and Analyse, the shape of the answer also matters. Bulleted lists and tables of statements cannot get most of the marks. The same is true for separate lists of benefits and drawbacks if each item is only one word or a very short sentence.

cites.quote: learners who produced bulleted lists or tables of statements were unable to access most of the marks
if these answers are shown in a sketched table, they do not properly answer the question as there is no e.g., discussion
This comment also applies to answers that have separate lists of benefits and drawbacks, but the lists consist of single word or very brief sentences.

points.text: The mark schemes once printed this rule too. From 2021 to 2023, almost every Paper 1 and Paper 3 mark scheme had a limit for bulleted answers to Discuss, Evaluate or Analyse questions. On an 8-mark question, the limit was 6 marks, however good the points were. Shorter questions had lower limits, for example 3 of 4 marks. In 2024, only the March and June Paper 3 mark schemes still printed the limit. From November 2024, the mark schemes do not print it. But the 2025 examiner reports still say that bulleted lists and tables cannot get most of the marks.

cites.quote: Max. six marks if bullets/list of points Must have expansions or comparisons to be a proper discussion
Max 6 marks if bullets/list of points.
five marks if bullets/list of points Must have expansions to be a proper analysis

points.text: Bullets are not completely banned. One Paper 1 question in November 2025 asked for the steps of planning something. The examiners accepted a list of steps, sometimes bulleted, or a description. Each step had to show a decision. Treat this as a rare exception. Everywhere else, the examiner reports ask for full sentences.

cites.quote: In the first, candidates listed (sometimes by creating a bulleted list) steps that would be taken, whilst others described the steps that had been taken. Either method was acceptable

points.text: You do not lose marks for grammar or spelling. Examiners give marks for correct points. They do not take marks away for errors. But your meaning must still be clear.

cites.quote: marks are not deducted for errors

answers should only be judged on the quality of spelling, punctuation and grammar when these features are specifically assessed by the question as indicated by the mark scheme. The meaning, however, should be unambiguous.

points.text: Short sentences are fine. Put one clear point in each sentence. This is easier for the examiner to mark and easier for you to check.

cites.quote: Keep most sentences short and focused. That will help with clarity and in making every point stand out for the examiner.

points.text: Some mark schemes give one mark for a point. They give a second mark only when you add its reason or detail. One mark scheme says clearly that an answer made only of bare points has a mark limit.

cites.quote: MAX two marks if answers are all only first marks.

points.text: Answer the question that the paper asks, about the scenario it gives. Do not write everything you know about one word that you saw in the question. That does not earn the marks.

cites.quote: the full range of marks is only available to candidates for answers referring to the scenario in the questions
Centres must ensure that candidates target their answers to the questions as they are written and not at ‘key’ words in the questions.

points.text: Do not write out mark scheme bullets that you learnt by heart. Examiners notice this. A list of learnt points does not answer a new question.

cites.quote: Examiners saw many scripts where candidates listed sets of bullet points that appeared to have been learnt directly from previous mark schemes.

points.text: Use the number of marks as a clue to how much to write. It tells you how many separate points, or how much detail, the examiner expects.

cites.quote: Look at how many marks are allocated to a question. This gives you a clue as to how much work is expected.
the number of marks available for each question is a useful indicator of how much detail or how many descriptions should be given in the answers

points.text: Never leave a question blank. A few sentences on a topic you are unsure of can still earn marks.

cites.quote: Writing a few sentences, even if little is known about the topic, may gain valuable marks towards the overall total.
